sbh2.6:2.6: The four-phase analysis (in-breath, pause-after-in, out-breath, pause-after-out) is more granular than what the Pali suttas give. MN 118 has just *assāsa* and *passāsa*. The Yogācāra refinement explicitly carves out the two pauses as part of the practice object — they are not 'gaps' between breaths but legitimate phases the practitioner attends to.
sbh2.6:3.14: An empirically grounded fact disguised as scholastic argument: the breath ceases in the fourth jhāna, in the cessation attainment, and does not begin until the embryo has developed past the *peśī* (fleshy-mass) stage. The takeaway: **in deep concentration the breath stops** — Asanga validates this canonically.
sbh2.6:4.11: The source ends this clause with a stray *pāḥ* — most plausibly an eroded fragment of the expected closing formula *iyamucyate sūkṣmasauṣiryam* ('this is called the subtle cavity'), with only the final visarga preserved. The Sanskrit is kept as found per [the emendation policy](../notes/sanskrit-emendation-policy.md); the English flags the corruption.
sbh2.6:5.3: The fourth name, *kāya-saṁskāra* (body-conditioner), is the term used in MN 118's third tetrad ('calming the body-conditioner, I breathe in'). Asanga signals the canonical anchor here.
sbh2.6:6.3: The root prints *aśithila-prayogatā* ('non-slack engagement'), but the explanation at 6.4 describes laziness, sloth-and-torpor, and outward distraction; the fault required by the paired contrast with over-tight engagement is slack engagement. The English marks this repair rather than silently reversing the printed form.
sbh2.6:6.11: A clinical observation. Forceful breath-control produces actual physical disturbances — beginning as palpitations or tics (*sphuraka* — 'throbber') and progressing to pain (*rujaka* — 'pain-maker'). The remedy isn't a separate technique — it's avoiding both extremes from the start.
sbh2.6:7.2: The spine of the Yogācāra breath practice: five progressive depths, each complete in itself, cumulative. Counting establishes stability. Aggregate-entry pivots breath into insight by analyzing the breath into the five aggregates. Dependent-origination-entry traces the conditional chain. Truth-entry generates the four noble truths. Sixteen-aspect-familiarity is the breath-practice sixteenfold sequence parallel to MN 118, not the four-truth *ṣoḍaśākāra* framework used elsewhere.
sbh2.6:9.28: A precise scaling protocol: one-per-breath (*ekaika*), then two-per-count, then four, then ten, eventually a hundred. Each scale-up permitted only when the mind doesn't drift in between — a graduated extension of the duration of attention.
sbh2.6:9.36: *svarasa-vāhin* — 'carried by its own essence.' Echoes stage 9 of the nine mental abidings (*svarasa-vāhana*). The practitioner has reached the point where the mind goes naturally on the breath — counting becomes unnecessary because attention is self-sustaining.
sbh2.6:9.46: Asanga explicitly says counting is the *training-wheel* for those who need it. For sharp-faculty practitioners, *priyārohatā* is treated here as easy uptake: they can quickly grasp the counting protocol and then move directly to attentive characterization of the breath. The modern question of whether counting is necessary gets a direct answer: only if the mind would otherwise drift.
sbh2.6:10.7: This is the pivot from *śamatha* into *vipaśyanā* applied to the breath. The breath is *rūpa*; the felt-tone of attending to it is *vedanā*; the recognizing 'this is in-breath' is *saṁjñā*; the mindfulness-intention-discernment present is *saṁskāra*; the bare cognizing is *vijñāna*. Breath becomes a fully analyzed phenomenological event.
sbh2.6:11.16: A compressed five-link chain (ignorance → previous-formations → life-faculty → body/consciousness → breath), focused on what makes breathing happen. At 11.10, *sarva-saṁskāra-pratyayaṁ jīvitendriyam* means the life-faculty is conditioned by formations; it should not be read as 'the previous formation conditioning all formations is the life-faculty.' Asanga grounds the abstract twelve-link doctrine in immediate experiential observation: *this very breath* depends on these conditions.
sbh2.6:12.5: *abhūtvā bhavanti, bhūtvā ca prativigacchanti* — 'not having been, they come to be; having come to be, they pass away.' The canonical Pali *anicca* refrain rendered into Sanskrit, anchoring the later final-tetrad move to 'contemplating impermanence.'
sbh2.6:15.10: Asanga's gloss on 'long/short' is unique. The 'long' breath is the standard in/out cycle. The 'short' breath is the *inner* in-breath and *inner* out-breath — the brief turnaround pauses. So 'long' and 'short' are not about duration but about which phase of respiration is the object. This resolves a long-standing ambiguity in MN 118.
sbh2.6:15.20: The printed/root phrase *sitām avasthām* is difficult. A literal 'white state' is contextually awkward in this breath-pause analysis, though *sitām* may be defensible if understood from √sī ('to bind') rather than as 'white.' The English therefore gives the likely functional sense — the still/resting interval-state empty of the moving in-breath and out-breath — while marking the line [Damaged/Conjectural]. Sanskrit JSON is left unchanged.
sbh2.6:15.25: An empirical observation: beginning practice produces breath that is *kharā, duḥsaṁsparśā* (rough, unpleasant-to-touch). Mature practice produces breath that is *mṛdavaḥ, sukha-saṁsparśāḥ* (soft, pleasant-to-touch). Every meditator notices this; Asanga grounds the sutta phrase 'calming the body-conditioner' in it.
sbh2.6:16.6: Breath practice is viable through the third jhāna; in the fourth, breath ceases (consistent with the earlier statement that fourth-jhāna attainers don't breathe). This bounds the applicability of *ānāpānasmṛti* by absorption level, without collapsing the sixteenfold breath sequence into the separate four-truth sixteen-aspect framework.
sbh2.6:17.5: Even in jhāna, the eight standard self-related conceptual moves can intrude — 'I am, I shall be, I shall not be, I shall be with form, without form, percipient, non-percipient, neither.' The practitioner abandons these at first sign. This is the *prapañca* (proliferation) detection mapped onto the third tetrad's 'calming the mental-formation.'
sbh2.6:18.13: The mind-tetrad operationalized as hindrance-management. Sloth-and-torpor calls for *gladdening*. Agitation-and-remorse calls for *concentrating*. When neither is present, the mind is *liberated* from hindrances. Same instruction as VSM Ch 4's balancing of faculties, applied here as breath-tetrad commentary.
sbh2.6:19.5: The transition is temporal: first *śamatha-yoga* supported by absorption or access, then direct *vipaśyanā* on impermanence at 19.6. The prior English fragment was not wrong in content, but it did not read as a sentence.
sbh2.6:19.9: Three 'elements' name the three remaining work-products of the path: *prahāṇa-dhātu* (abandoning, for seeing-abandonable defilements), *virāga-dhātu* (dispassion, for cultivation-abandonable defilements), *nirodha-dhātu* (cessation, for the bases of clinging). *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* on the breath with these as aim brings the mind to liberation.
sbh2.6:20.2: Breath practice, fully matured through the five familiarities, yields *arhatship*. The same claim MN 118 makes. The sixteen aspects, properly developed, are sufficient for full liberation.
sbh2.6:21.3: The source phrase *savyokṣepamadhyātmaṁ pratyātmaṁ āsannāsannaṁ* is unstable. The current English keeps the likely functional sense — the breath object is inward, one's own, and very near, so it does not provoke applied-thought agitation in an applied-thought-conduct person — but marks the line [Damaged/Conjectural] rather than presenting the parse as secure.
